name: Dairy Bar and Durham Train Station
place: Dairy Bar and Durham Train Station
use: Amtrak Downeaster station (waiting room) and the UNH Dairy Bar café, now open summers only
builtText: Built 1896 in Lynn, Mass.; dismantled and re-erected in Durham 1911–12
statusNote: Amtrak station open year-round; Dairy Bar café paused for the academic year, open summers

renovations.what: Depot rehabilitated as an intermodal center (reopened Aug. 11, 2008): slate roof repaired, semaphore restored, marble floors and woodwork repaired, mechanical/electrical systems replaced, ADA restrooms, heated vestibule, separate entrances for waiting room and Dairy Bar, bus roundabout

facts.text: The depot was first built in 1896 as the East Lynn station in Lynn, Massachusetts; the Boston & Maine took it apart and rebuilt it in Durham when it moved its tracks west of campus in 1911–12.
The railroad moved the line after a January 1905 derailment in the middle of campus.
UNH bought the depot from the Boston & Maine for $1 on September 28, 1960, and opened the Dairy Bar in it in 1965.
Passenger trains stopped serving Durham on June 30, 1967; service returned with the Amtrak Downeaster on December 14, 2001.
Buff brick walls rise from a rusticated brown granite base, with round arches trimmed in granite, carved foliage capitals, and hipped slate roofs over the depot and its trackside canopy.

The $940,000 2008 rehabilitation was paid for mostly by Federal Highway Administration programs ($668,000 CMAQ, $84,000 Transportation Enhancement) plus $188,000 from UNH, and won a New Hampshire Preservation Alliance award in 2009.
UNH Dining paused the Dairy Bar's regular operations for the academic year from December 17, citing sales that have declined since COVID-19 and unsustainable losses; it reopens for summer.
In summer 2026 the Dairy Bar was open weekdays from June 1 to August 21.
The station is owned by UNH and is the third-busiest Amtrak stop in New Hampshire.

verdict: An 1896 Romanesque depot moved here from Lynn in 1912, bought by UNH for $1: a well-kept small gem and the town's front door.
notes: Category kept as dining, but the building is equally the Amtrak station; the waiting room stays open with train service while the café is seasonal. Re-erection year differs by source: Great American Stations says the depot arrived 1911, Wikipedia and the Archives say 1912. The closure notice (s4) gives 'December 17' with no year; the old row dated it Dec 2025, consistent with the summer-2026 reopening (s5). No licensed interior photo of the marble-floored waiting room or the café was found; all licensed photos are exteriors (warm buff brick, granite arches, slate roof, generous canopy; the street side is cluttered with utility poles and wires). Windows are deep round-arched, so interior light is probably moderate. A/C not documented. Architect of the 1896 Lynn depot not confirmed.
judgeNotes: Photos confirm buff brick, granite arches and slate roofs, though parking and poles crowd the views. Exterior down a point from the old run on that basis.
